subject: Culture
title: Wedding Colors
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Wedding Colors.

hook.text: White wedding dresses only became tradition after Queen Victoria wore one in 1840. Before that, any color worked.

buildup.text: In China, red is the wedding color. It symbolizes luck, prosperity, and joy.

discovery.text: Indian brides wear red or gold. White is for funerals. Wearing white to an Indian wedding is a grave mistake.

twist.text: Globalization is spreading white dresses worldwide. Japanese, Chinese, and Indian brides now sometimes wear white too.

climax.text: Wedding color carries centuries of meaning. Changing it changes the story the bride tells.

punchline.text: A queen's fashion choice became the world's tradition.

quiz.question: Who popularized the white wedding dress in 1840?

details.summary: Wedding color traditions vary dramatically worldwide. White dominates Western weddings since Queen Victoria, but Chinese brides wear red for luck, Indian brides wear red or gold, and Japanese brides change outfits from white to red during the ceremony to symbolize transformation.
details.whyItMatters: Wedding colors encode cultural values about purity, luck, fertility, and transformation. Understanding them prevents cross-cultural misunderstandings at one of life's most emotionally significant events.
takeaways: White wedding dresses were popularized by Queen Victoria in 1840
Chinese brides traditionally wear red to symbolize luck and prosperity
Indian wedding attire features red, gold, and elaborate embroidery

faq.question: Why do Chinese brides wear red?
faq.answer: Red symbolizes luck, prosperity, happiness, and fertility in Chinese culture. It wards off evil spirits and represents the fire element. Traditional Chinese wedding dress (qipao or kua) features elaborate red and gold embroidery with phoenix and dragon motifs.

faq.question: Why did Western brides not always wear white?
faq.answer: Before Queen Victoria wore white in 1840, brides simply wore their best dress in any color. White fabric was expensive and impractical — it showed every stain and could not be re-worn easily. Victoria's wealthy, photogenic choice was widely publicized and gradually became the standard.
